notes.urn:cts:latinLit:phi0474.phi039.perseus-: 'He' in the first sentence is Gnaeus Sicinius, named in the preceding section; from 'His memory' on, the subject is Curio, whose oratory is under discussion. 'Titinia Cottae': her relation to Cotta (wife or daughter) is not stated.

nodes.text: When he, as tribune of the plebs, had brought the consuls Curio and Octavius before the people, and Curio had spoken at length while his colleague Gnaeus Octavius sat by — who was bound up in bandages and smeared with many ointments because of pain in his joints — he said: 'Octavius, you will never be able to repay your colleague: if he had not thrown himself about in his usual way, the flies would have eaten you up there today.' His memory, moreover, was so nonexistent that sometimes, when he had set out three points, he would either add a fourth or be looking for the third; and in a private trial, one of the very greatest, when I had made the closing speech for Cotta's Titinia, and he was to speak against me for Servius Naevius, he suddenly forgot the whole case, and he said that this had been brought about by Titinia's potions and spells.
